query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Refining the dual-phase lamellar colonies by applying moderate rolling and short sub-critical annealing can reduce dislocation pile-ups, alleviating boundary stress concentrations and preventing microcracking, thus significantly improving room-temperature ductility while maintaining or slightly increasing strength compared to the as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast (or as-solidified) eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical, dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
generation.intervention: Perform ~30–50% cold (or warm) rolling followed by a brief, sub-critical annealing treatment to refine the lamellar morphology and partially recrystallize the microstructure.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile loading for performance assessment; standard ambient atmosphere for testing and moderate-temperature industrial applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellae and colony boundary spacing, with partial recrystallization leading to smaller, uniformly distributed grains/phases.
generation.mechanism: Decreasing lamellar spacing and generating finer substructures reduces effective slip length and decreases dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries, which lowers stress concentrations. In turn, microcrack initiation is suppressed, delaying catastrophic failure. Meanwhile, retained boundary and precipitation strengthening mechanisms preserve or slightly improve yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Ductility (e.g., ∼10–15% elongation at failure) increases compared to the starting state, and yield/ultimate tensile strengths are maintained or moderately enhanced due to refined microstructure.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy material exhibiting limited room-temperature ductility (e.g., <10% elongation) and moderate yield strength.
generation.boundary: Excessive rolling or annealing times/temperatures may cause over-recrystallization and grain growth, reducing strength. Insufficient rolling/annealing may under-refine lamellae, limiting ductility improvement.
generation.uncertainty: Exact tensile values depend on the alloy’s composition and the specific thermomechanical parameters (roll ratio, annealing temperature, and hold time).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare test coupons from the as-cast eutectic HEA and subject half to 30–50% rolling plus short-term sub-critical annealing. Compare mechanical properties to those of the as-cast controls using consistent room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Fractography via SEM/TEM to examine microcrack initiation sites and track dislocation structures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not exhibit a notable increase in tensile ductility along with retention or improvement of strength compared to the as-cast state, the hypothesis is falsified.

The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Figure 1(b) charts the processing route followed to obtain different microstructures and resulting properties. The as cast alloy was homogenized at 1150 °C for 1 h to annihilate the dislocations and reduce micro-segregations from casting process to assist in cold deformation of the alloy. The SEM microstructure from this condition is shown in Fig. 1(a). The backscattered electron diffraction (BSED) image in Fig. 1(a) shows a two phase eutectic type of microstructure with a bright contrast phase and dark contrast phase organized in lamellar arrangement. The grain boundaries are highlighted by the yellow lines and lamellae directions are shown using red arrows in the figure. The alloy was then rolled at room temperature to 30% reduction in thickness. chosen.technique: cold/warm rolling followed by sub-critical annealing
chosen.conditions: room-temperature tensile testing and possible elevated-temperature service; controlled rolling reductions (e.g., ~30–50%) and short annealing
chosen.why: Refining the lamellar colony structure via controlled deformation and short-term annealing reduces the length scale of microstructural boundaries, thereby alleviating dislocation pile-ups and the resulting local stress concentrations. This approach retains or even enhances strength through grain and colony-boundary strengthening while significantly improving ductility by mitigating boundary-driven crack initiation. It is a well-established, single-step route in materials processing and directly answers the need to counter limited room-temperature ductility and brittleness in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
